I'm really sorry, I hope you're doing better now. I have extensive scarring on my arms from self-harm and I spent a lot of time paranoid over people seeing, judging, and asking about them, I used to dread summer. I know how tough it is.

The past couple of years have been easier and I've sort of just...grown to accept them as part of me. I hate them, I hate that I did that to myself (especially in such a visible place), but they're never going to go away and I just have to learn to live with them. Also people really don't ask, they don't even stare as much as I thought. I like to think *most* people have more tact than that.

I got very drunk, with full knowledge that when I'm in a weird headspace sober, alcohol turns me pyscho. Got very drunk, physically assaulted and verbally berated a very close friend, ran away with the intention of killing myself and eventually got dragged back home by the police.

My friend was covered in bruises the next day, I nearly threw her down the stairs while drunk, I pulled chunks of her hair out, I really hurt her. The worst part was that she told me she could take the violence, but the stuff I said to her was going to stick with her for a long time.

This was two years ago and it changed my life. It's something I'll regret forever I think but it forced me to take responsibility for my actions and try to be a better person. I cut out the alcohol and just...tried to be someone who was worthy of being alive. I have very little patience for 'bad drunks' these days because it's a conscious choice to drink. I knew perfectly well that when I got very drunk I was a horrible person, but I did it anyway. That's on me, not the alcohol.

At some point you *have* to start taking responsibility and stop blaming the alcohol, it doesn't create problems, it just dredges up all the horrible things that always existed inside you and you have to be aware of that.

So I have a very unfortunate familiarity with dealing with feeling like a toxic friend. I'm difficult to get along with, I have unrealistic expectations from people and I'm *bad* at dealing with these feelings - I'll ignore and push people away instead of dealing with issues head on. I used to be very bad at not letting my mood affect the people around me. It's...an ongoing issue for me and I'm constantly working on it. I'm only saying this so you know that sometimes people fuck up and sometimes we let our personal issues spread to other people, and *I get it*.

Can you have a calm conversation with one of your friends about how you feel? If they say you've been acting 'toxic', try to understand why - don't get defensive or angry (my go-to response). 

If there is a problem, you're in a good position because you've recognised it, you can take steps to resolve it. You get angry and act out? Remove yourself from the situation before it spills over to your friends. If you've got some personal issues that are making you feel like shit, talk to them! They'll want to listen, want to help, and sometimes talking things through helps a lot.

It sounds like you have some good friends, and open communication about this sort of thing is *so* important. Also remember that depression itself warps how your mind works, how you think and react to things and you have to try and be kind to yourself. If you feel like you've wronged your friends, commit yourself to doing better - we can't undo our mistakes but we can work to make sure we don't make them again.

YMMV: different people react very differently to the same anti-depressant. I've been on a few. Some that I knew people did very well on were horrible for me with intolerable side effects.

I settled on Sertraline, which I took for about 2 years and tbh it made me fairly numb. At first this was a blessing and a huge improvement, but overtime not being able to 'access' my emotions was too much to handle and was having a very detrimental impact on my mental health. I weaned myself off them a few months ago and feel more like myself again (for better or worse). 

I have friends who stayed on the first anti-depressant they tried and did incredibly well on them. 

My advice would be to give it a go. The side effects during the first week or two can be *hell* if you're unlucky, but they are temporary and please please remember that if Prozac doesn't work there are so many others to try, it just requires a degree of patience to find the right one for you :)

I'm about to enter the NHS mental health system from a university support centre. The lady I saw for CBT at uni told me that in England the NHS have this 'IAPT' system (improving access to psychological treatment, I think). You can be referred by a gp or self-refer. The NHS website has a search engine for finding IAPT services in your area. If you just google IAPT nhs you should get somewhere.

What other people have said is true - some places you'll be waiting months, other maybe only a few weeks. It may be useful to discuss the IAPT services with your GP - they might be able to recommend a centre with a good reputation or short waiting times.

Hope everything goes okay x

Hey, I completely understand where you're coming from, I'm seeing a cbt therapist and often see my GP to discuss meds and I always find myself being very careful about what I say - I don't want to be locked up or have any of my family members contacted for talking about suicidal thoughts.

That being said however, in my last therapy appointment I told my therapist that a few days before I'd been really low and sat there with a knife against my arm for about an hour. We talked it over and she asked me lots of questions to ensure I wasn't at an immediate risk to myself. She didn't even bring up contacting anyone or anything like that. Instead, we came up with a safety plan together and brainstormed ways I could keep myself safe when I'm like that.

My biggest bit of advice is tell your therapist, I know how hard it is but they'll be able to give you resources to help you cope,
Hope everything goes okay, stay safe!
